bodies.linkedin:
A character error rate of 1% (99% accuracy) may result in an error rate of 5% or worse if word context is not used.

Optical character recognition has evolved from early telegraphic experiments into a technology used to digitize printed text for electronic editing and searching. While modern tools like Tesseract 5 or TrOCR assist in this process, the underlying mechanics often rely on binarization, as most commercial recognition algorithms work only on binary images.

Techniques such as near-neighbor analysis can help correct errors by utilizing co-occurrence frequencies of words. For specialized tasks, some software uses a two-pass approach where high-confidence results from the first pass improve recognition of remaining letters. Even with these methods, recognition of typewritten Latin script is not 100% accurate. Users can set confidence rates to trigger notifications for manual review when the system encounters uncertainty.

OCR technology can capture up to 99.91% of data.
bodies.thread:
OCR software can be used to defeat or test the robustness of CAPTCHA anti-bot systems.

Early experiments in the field included the Optophone, a handheld scanner that produced tones corresponding to characters, developed by Edmund Fournier d'Albe.

In 1931, Emanuel Goldberg was granted US Patent number 1,838,389 for a statistical machine used to search microfilm archives.

By January 13, 1976, Ray Kurzweil unveiled a reading machine for the blind that included a flatbed scanner and a text-to-speech synthesizer.

Commercial OCR software accuracy for 19th- and early 20th-century newspaper pages varied from 81% to 99%.

A character error rate of 1% (99% accuracy) may result in an error rate of 5% or worse if word context is not used.

OCR technology has evolved from early mechanical experiments into a versatile way to digitize, search, and process text across diverse formats and applications.
